components.note: Woman — beauty and appearance are often linked to this root.
Gives the sound cì, related to zī but drifted apart over time.
力 (strength) — 势 relates to power, force, and influence
执 (zhí) gives a loose sound connection to 势's reading shì

example.hanzi: 瑜伽老师纠正了我的姿势。
example.pinyin: Yújiā lǎoshī jiūzhèng le wǒ de zīshì.
example.english: The yoga teacher corrected my posture.
example.fact: 姿势 refers to a concrete physical posture — how a body is positioned in space, as in exercise or photos — while its near-synonym 姿态 leans more abstract, covering overall bearing, stance, or attitude (political 姿态, for instance) as well as physical carriage.

components.note: 宀 (roof) — 宇 originally named the eaves of a house, extending outward in meaning to 'the universe.'
于 (yú) gives a sound close to yǔ, sharing the same syllable body and differing mainly in tone.
宀 (roof) — 宙 extends the idea of a roof overhead to the vastness of time and space, 'the universe.'
由 (yóu) shares the rhyme -ou with zhòu, though the initial has drifted from y- to zh- over time.

example.hanzi: 科学家一直在研究宇宙的起源。
example.pinyin: Kēxuéjiā yìzhí zài yánjiū yǔzhòu de qǐyuán.
example.english: Scientists have been studying the origin of the universe.
example.fact: 宇 originally named the eaves of a house — the outer edge of a bounded space — while 宙 referred to the passage of time within that same dwelling; 宇宙 fuses the two into "all of space" plus "all of time," an image that maps naturally onto the modern physics notion of spacetime, centuries before the term existed in Chinese.

components.note: 面 was originally a pictograph of a human face, with an outline around an eye — later broadening to mean 'face, surface, side.'
讠 (speech) — 试 relates to proposing or trying something out
式 (shì) gives the sound — an exact match with 试's pronunciation shì

example.hanzi: 她明天要去参加一个面试。
example.pinyin: Tā míngtiān yào qù cānjiā yí gè miànshì.
example.english: She has a job interview to attend tomorrow.
example.fact: 面试 (literally "face test") is paired with 笔试 ("pen test," a written exam) as the two-part vocabulary Chinese uses to distinguish an in-person interview from a written test — both compounds share 试, the character for "to try, to test."

components.note: 日 (sun) — 最 pictures something happening under the sun, that is, everywhere.
取 (to take, gather) — combined with the sun above, gathering everything under the sun gave 最 its meaning of 'most' or 'the utmost.'
亲 (here representing a tree, related to 榛/hazel) — 新 pictures a tree being cut.
斤 (an axe) — freshly chopping wood gave 新 its meaning of something 'new' or 'fresh.'

example.hanzi: 这是这个品牌最新的手机型号。
example.pinyin: Zhè shì zhège pǐnpái zuìxīn de shǒujī xínghào.
example.english: This is the brand's latest phone model.
example.fact: 最 functions as Mandarin's all-purpose superlative marker — stuck directly onto almost any adjective (最好 "best," 最大 "biggest," 最新 "newest") — doing the job that English splits between the suffix "-est" and the separate word "most."

components.note: 臣 here pictures a large, downcast eye, an old image tied to lying down or resting.
卜 (an altered form of 人, 'person') completes the picture of someone lying in bed, giving 卧 its meaning 'to lie down.'
宀 (roof) — 室 refers to an enclosed room under a roof
至 (zhì) gives the sound — an exact match with 室's reading shì

example.hanzi: 他家有两个卧室。
example.pinyin: Tā jiā yǒu liǎng gè wòshì.
example.english: His home has two bedrooms.
example.fact: 卧室 literally means "lying-down room" — 卧 pictures a person reclining, and 室 is a roofed, enclosed chamber — a transparent compound that singles out the bedroom specifically, in contrast to the generic 房间 ("room") that covers any room in the house.

components.note: 辶 (walking/movement) — relates to 远's meaning 'far, distant,' a long way to walk.
元 (yuán) gives a sound hint — 远 is pronounced yuǎn, sharing the same base sound with a different tone.
亠 — read as the head of an animal standing upright in this pictograph; the character was later reused for the unrelated meaning 'to leave, be apart from, distance.'

example.hanzi: 医生建议他远离辛辣的食物。
example.pinyin: Yīshēng jiànyì tā yuǎnlí xīnlà de shíwù.
example.english: The doctor advised him to stay away from spicy food.
example.fact: 远离 works as a transitive verb — 远离 + object — for both physical and figurative distance ("stay away from spicy food," "get away from your phone"), a construction the plain adjective 远 ("far") can't form on its own, since 远 needs a coverb like 离 to attach to a following noun.

components.note: 刂 (knife) contributes to the character's form, though its link to 剧's meaning 'drama' has faded over time.
居 (jū) gives a rhyme close to jù, with the tone shifted.
木 (tree) — provides the base image of a tree.
一 (a line) marks the base of the trunk, highlighting the roots — giving 本 its meaning 'root, origin, source.'

example.hanzi: 这部电影的剧本改编自一本小说。
example.pinyin: Zhèbù diànyǐng de jùběn gǎibiān zì yì běn xiǎoshuō.
example.english: This movie's screenplay is adapted from a novel.
example.fact: 本 alone can mean "book," "edition," or the measure word for bound volumes (一本书), and 剧本 literally reads as "the drama's book" — the written text a play, film, or TV series is built from, the same 本 pattern behind 课本 ("textbook") and 日记本 ("diary").

components.note: 讠 (speech) — relates to 请's meaning 'to request, invite; please,' a spoken request.
青 (qīng) gives a sound hint — 请 is pronounced qǐng, sharing the same base sound with a different tone.
口 (mouth) — 问 relates to speaking, specifically asking a question.
门 (mén) gives a hint of the sound — 问 is pronounced wèn, related but the tone and vowel have shifted.

example.hanzi: 请问,洗手间在哪里?
example.pinyin: Qǐngwèn, xǐshǒujiān zài nǎlǐ?
example.english: Excuse me, where is the restroom?
example.fact: 请问 is a fixed opening formula — it always precedes a question, never a statement — functioning like English "excuse me, but..." or "may I ask..." to politely address a stranger before asking directions, a favor, or information.

components.note: 手 is a simple picture of an open hand with the fingers spread out.
扌 (hand) — 指 relates to using the hand, specifically the fingers.
旨 (an aim, purpose) — combined with 扌 (hand), 指 came to mean 'finger' and 'to point,' aiming the hand at something.

example.hanzi: 小孩用手指指着天上的月亮。
example.pinyin: Xiǎohái yòng shǒuzhǐ zhǐzhe tiānshàng de yuèliang.
example.english: The child pointed at the moon in the sky with their finger.
example.fact: 指 does double duty as both a noun meaning "finger" and a verb meaning "to point" — sensible since pointing is literally done with a finger — so 手指 (the noun "finger") and 指 (the verb "to point," as in 指着 "pointing at") share the same root character.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — the act of speaking.
正 (straight, correct) — speaking the straight, correct truth, giving 证 its meaning 'to prove, certify; evidence.'

example.hanzi: 警方已经证实了这个消息。
example.pinyin: Jǐngfāng yǐjīng zhèngshí le zhège xiāoxi.
example.english: The police have already confirmed this piece of news.
example.fact: 证实 specifically means to verify that a claim or report is objectively true, often through evidence or investigation — common in news and police contexts — while its near-synonym 确认 leans toward administrative confirmation, like confirming a booking or acknowledging receipt of a message.

components.note: 辶 (to walk) shows movement.
万 (ten thousand, suggesting a great distance) shows a big stride, giving 迈 its meaning 'to step, to stride.'
阝 (a mound/place) — reflects 阿's original meaning related to a hill or slope
可 (kě) gives a sound close to 阿's reading ā
宓 depicts stillness and quiet beneath a roof.
山 (mountain) — a quiet, secluded mountain gave 密 its meaning 'dense, secret, close.'

example.hanzi: 他们计划明年去迈阿密旅行。
example.pinyin: Tāmen jìhuà míngnián qù Mài'āmì lǚxíng.
example.english: They are planning to travel to Miami next year.
example.fact: 迈阿密 is a pure phonetic transliteration of the English "Miami" — 迈 ("to stride"), 阿 (a meaningless filler syllable common across transliterated foreign names, as in 阿富汗 "Afghanistan"), and 密 ("dense, secret") are borrowed only for their sounds, not their meanings, the same strategy behind virtually all foreign place names in Chinese.

components.note: A single horizontal stroke — the simplest possible way to represent the number one; some traditional interpretations link it to heaven or earth as the very first stroke of creation.
足 (foot) — relates to 路's meaning 'road, path,' something walked on with feet.
各 (gè) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from lù.

example.hanzi: 祝你一路平安!
example.pinyin: Zhù nǐ yílù píng'ān!
example.english: Wishing you a safe journey!
example.fact: 一路 anchors a whole family of travel farewells — 一路平安 ("safe travels") and 一路顺风 ("smooth journey," literally "wind at your back the whole way") — the fixed phrases Chinese speakers reach for when seeing someone off on a trip.

components.note: 贝 (shell/money) — 资 relates to wealth, funds, and resources.
次 (cì) gives a hint of the sound — 资 is pronounced zī, a connection that has shifted significantly over time.
木 (wood) — 格 originally meant a wooden branch or standard, extended to 'pattern, style, rule.'
各 (gè) gives a sound hint — 格 is pronounced gé, sharing the same rhyme with a different tone.

example.hanzi: 他没有参加这次考试的资格。
example.pinyin: Tā méiyǒu cānjiā zhècì kǎoshì de zīgé.
example.english: He doesn't have the qualifications to take this exam.
example.fact: 资格 shows up constantly in the pattern 有/没有...的资格 ("to have/not have the standing to...") — used for formal eligibility, like exam qualifications, but just as often rhetorically, as in 你没有资格说这话 ("you have no right to say that").

components.note: 亻 (person) plus 乍 (suddenly/for the first time) — together suggesting a person making or doing something for the first time.
宀 (roof) — 家 is about a home, the space under a roof.
豕 (shǐ, 'pig') supplies the ancient sound for 家; keeping a pig under one's roof was also a practical sign of a household in ancient China, though the modern readings jiā and shǐ no longer rhyme.

example.hanzi: 她是一位很有名的作家。
example.pinyin: Tā shì yí wèi hěn yǒumíng de zuòjiā.
example.english: She is a very famous author.
example.fact: 家 (literally "home, family") has broadened into a suffix marking expertise or profession — 作家 ("writer"), 画家 ("painter"), 科学家 ("scientist") — functioning much like English "-er" or "-ist" tacked onto a field of activity.

components.note: 辛 (bitter, harsh) — 辞 describes speech that carries a sharp edge.
舌 (tongue) — bitter 辛 words spoken by the tongue 舌 gave 辞 its meaning 'words, speech,' and later 'to resign, to take leave.'
耳 (ear) — an old link between listening to official duties and 职's meaning 'duty, profession, office'
只 (zhī) gives a loose sound connection to 职's reading zhí

example.hanzi: 他因为压力太大决定辞职。
example.pinyin: Tā yīnwèi yālì tài dà juédìng cízhí.
example.english: He decided to resign because the pressure was too great.
example.fact: 辞职 is a verb-object compound — 辞 ("to resign from") plus its own built-in object 职 ("post") — so it's already grammatically "full" and can't take a further direct object; naming a specific job requires inserting another verb, as in 辞去这个职位 ("resign from this position"), rather than tacking the job directly onto 辞职.

components.note: 衤 (clothing) — 被 originally meant a quilt or covering, like a blanket.
皮 (pí) gives a hint of the sound — 被 is pronounced bèi, a connection that has shifted over time.
口 (mouth) — the act of speaking.
牛 (ox) — traditionally read as speaking with the forceful weight of an ox, giving 告 its meaning 'to tell, announce, inform.'

example.hanzi: 被告在法庭上保持沉默。
example.pinyin: Bèigào zài fǎtíng shàng bǎochí chénmò.
example.english: The defendant remained silent in court.
example.fact: 被 is Mandarin's passive marker (被 + verb = "to be verbed," as in 被打 "to be hit"), so 被告 literally parses as "the one who is accused" — built the same way as any passive construction — and pairs with its courtroom counterpart 原告 ("the plaintiff," literally "the original accuser").

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 钱 relates to money, since early Chinese coins were made of metal
戋 (jiān) gives a loose sound connection to 钱's reading qián
勹 (an enclosing shape) — wrapping around.
巳 (a baby) — swaddled inside, the image of wrapping something up giving 包 its meaning 'to wrap; bag, package.'

example.hanzi: 我的钱包不见了!
example.pinyin: Wǒ de qiánbāo bú jiàn le!
example.english: My wallet is missing!
example.fact: 钱包 is about as transparent as compounds get: 钱 ("money," built on the metal radical 钅 since early coins were cast in bronze) plus 包 ("bag," a pictograph of something wrapped up) combine literally into "money bag" — the everyday word for wallet or purse.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 诚 relates to speaking honestly and sincerely.
成 (chéng) gives the sound — an exact match with 诚's reading chéng.

example.hanzi: 做人要诚实,不能说谎。
example.pinyin: Zuò rén yào chéngshí, bù néng shuōhuǎng.
example.english: One should be honest and not tell lies.
example.fact: 诚实 describes honesty as a straightforward moral virtue — telling the truth, not lying — while its near-synonym 老实 overlaps in meaning but leans toward "well-behaved, guileless, simple," sometimes carrying a faint hint of naivety that 诚实 doesn't have.

components.note: 贝 (currency, wealth) sits on the left.
戋 means 'small, little' — paired with money 贝, this pictures something costing very little, giving 贱 its meaning 'cheap, of low value.'
A simple line drawing of a person's legs seen from the side, used to depict a human being.

example.hanzi: 电视剧里,女主角气得骂对方是贱人。
example.pinyin: Diànshìjù lǐ, nǚzhǔjué qì de mà duìfāng shì jiànrén.
example.english: In the TV drama, the female lead got so angry she called the other woman a "jiànrén."
example.fact: 贱人 is a strongly vulgar, gendered insult, roughly equivalent to "bitch" or "slut" — 贱 ("cheap, lowly, contemptible") plus 人 ("person") combine into a term that gained extra circulation in China through internet slang and viral video clips in the 2010s, and it should be recognized as a genuine insult rather than ordinary vocabulary.

components.note: 氵 (water/stream) — water naturally follows a fixed course, an image linked to the idea of 'law' or 'method.'
去 (to go/a course) — the path a stream follows suggested a regulated, consistent way of doing things, hence 'law, method.'

example.hanzi: 这种做法在很多国家都是合法的。
example.pinyin: Zhèzhǒng zuòfǎ zài hěn duō guójiā dōu shì héfǎ de.
example.english: This practice is legal in many countries.
example.fact: 合法 (literally "conforming to law" — 合 "to match, fit" plus 法 "law") pairs with its direct opposite 非法 ("illegal"), formed with the negating prefix 非-, the same prefix behind other formal antonyms like 非正式 ("informal") and 非官方 ("unofficial").

components.note: 米 (grain) — 粉 names a fine powder, originally made by grinding grain.
分 (fēn) gives a sound very close to fěn, sharing the initial and rhyme — only the tone differs.
纟 (thread) — 丝 is a simplified picture of two twisted strands of silk thread.

example.hanzi: 他是那个歌手的忠实粉丝。
example.pinyin: Tā shì nàge gēshǒu de zhōngshí fěnsī.
example.english: He is that singer's devoted fan.
example.fact: 粉丝 first meant only mung-bean noodles; its now-dominant sense of "fan, enthusiast" arose only in the 2000s as a phonetic pun on the English word "fans," which happens to sound almost identical — the food meaning came first, and the fandom meaning was borrowed wholesale from English sound alone.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 谢 describes an act of speaking, giving thanks.
射 (shè) gives the sound — an exact match with 谢.
大 (a person, arms outstretched) — represents a human being.
一 (a line, here representing the sky) — drawn above a person, showing what is above them: the heavens, hence 'sky, day.'
讠 (speech) — 谢 describes an act of speaking, giving thanks.
射 (shè) gives the sound — an exact match with 谢.
土 (earth/soil) — 地's original meaning is 'earth, ground'
也 (yě) gives a partial sound match for 地's other reading dì; in this grammatical-particle usage the character is instead pronounced 'de'

example.hanzi: 谢天谢地,飞机没有延误。
example.pinyin: Xiètiānxièdì, fēijī méiyǒu yánwù.
example.english: Thank goodness, the flight wasn't delayed.
example.fact: 谢天谢地 literally means "thank heaven, thank earth" — repeating 谢 ("to thank") across both halves of the fixed cosmic pair 天地 ("heaven and earth") — a structure with prayer-like origins that today functions as a purely secular exclamation of relief, much like English "thank goodness."

meanings: (reduplicated, in an urgent plea) please help!

components.note: 攵 (a hand taking action) — 救 describes the act of rescuing someone.
求 (qiú) gives a sound close to jiù, sharing a similar rhyme.
攵 (a hand taking action) — 救 describes the act of rescuing someone.
求 (qiú) gives a sound close to jiù, sharing a similar rhyme.

example.hanzi: 妈妈,救救我!
example.pinyin: Māma, jiùjiu wǒ!
example.english: Mom, save me!
example.fact: 救救 doubles the single verb 救 ("to save, to rescue") using Mandarin's common VV reduplication pattern — the same pattern that softens a casual request in 看看 ("take a quick look") — but attached to an urgent verb like 救, it instead reads as a plaintive, pleading cry, as in the common exclamation 救救我!("please save me!").

meanings: to search (a place, a database, online etc)

components.note: 扌 (hand) shows 搜 relates to physically searching for something.
叟 (sǒu) gives a sound close to sōu, differing mainly in tone.
糸 (thread) — thick strands twisted into a rope
冖 (a covering) — the ceiling or beam the rope hangs from

example.hanzi: 你可以在网上搜索这个问题的答案。
example.pinyin: Nǐ kěyǐ zài wǎngshàng sōusuǒ zhège wèntí de dá'àn.
example.english: You can search online for the answer to this question.
example.fact: 搜索 is the more formal, technical register of "to search" — the word printed on search-engine buttons and used for database queries or police searches — while everyday casual speech more often reaches for the plainer 查 or 找 to mean the same basic idea of looking something up.

components.note: 女 (woman) — represents a mother.
子 (child/son) — a mother together with her child was seen as an image of goodness, giving 好 its meaning 'good.'

example.hanzi: 好久不见,你最近怎样?
example.pinyin: Hǎojiǔ bú jiàn, nǐ zuìjìn zěnyàng?
example.english: Long time no see, how have you been lately?
example.fact: 好久不见 ("long time no see") is one of Mandarin's standard reunion greetings — and the near word-for-word English phrase "long time no see" is widely believed to be a calque borrowed directly from this Chinese expression by Chinese immigrant communities, rather than a coincidence.

components.note: 工 depicts a carpenter's square or workman's tool — a simple shape that came to represent work and labor.

example.hanzi: 这家工厂生产各种电子产品。
example.pinyin: Zhèjiā gōngchǎng shēngchǎn gèzhǒng diànzǐ chǎnpǐn.
example.english: This factory produces all kinds of electronic products.
example.fact: 厂 by itself is a simplified pictograph of a bare lean-to shelter — strokes suggesting a roof over an open space — so 工厂 literally reads as "a building for work," with 厂 also showing up as a component in other structure-related simplified characters like 广.

components.note: 纟 (thread/silk) — 给 originally related to supplying thread or material, later broadening to mean 'to give.'
合 (hé) gives a hint of the sound — 给 is pronounced gěi, a connection that has shifted over time.

example.hanzi: 妈妈把最后一块蛋糕留给了我。
example.pinyin: Māma bǎ zuìhòu yí kuài dàngāo liúgěi le wǒ.
example.english: Mom saved the last piece of cake for me.
example.fact: 留给 attaches the complement 给 ("to, for") onto the verb 留 ("to keep, leave behind") specifically to name a recipient — commonly slotted into the 把...留给... construction ("set X aside for Y"), a verb-complement pattern that makes clear who the leftover or saved item is meant for.

components.note: 土 (here representing a person swinging their arms, not its usual meaning 'earth') — depicts someone in motion.
止 (a foot) — combined with the moving figure above, 走 shows a person walking or running.
辶 (walking/movement) — relates to 运's meaning 'to move, transport,' and by extension 'fortune,' the movement of one's life.
云 (yún) gives a sound hint — 运 is pronounced yùn, sharing the same base sound with a different tone.

example.hanzi: 今天真走运,我捡到了一百块钱。
example.pinyin: Jīntiān zhēn zǒuyùn, wǒ jiǎndào le yìbǎi kuài qián.
example.english: I got really lucky today — I found a hundred yuan.
example.fact: 运 carries both "to move, transport" and "fortune, destiny" as core senses (as in 运气, "luck"), so 走运 pictures good fortune as something that walks toward you — paired with the opposite construction 倒霉 ("to have bad luck"), where 倒 means "to fall, overturn," picturing misfortune instead as something toppling over.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 吸 describes breathing in through the mouth.
及 (jí) reflects the character's historical phonetic root, though the modern reading xī has diverged.
龶 depicts a poisonous plant, tying 毒 to its meaning 'poison.'
母 (mǔ) gives a rhyme close to dú, with the initial shifted.

example.hanzi: 吸毒对身体的伤害非常大。
example.pinyin: Xīdú duì shēntǐ de shānghài fēicháng dà.
example.english: Drug use causes very serious harm to the body.
example.fact: 吸毒 literally means "to inhale poison" — 吸 ("to breathe in") plus 毒 ("poison, toxin") — a compound rooted in inhaling or smoking a substance, even though the word is now used broadly for illegal drug use regardless of whether it's actually inhaled, injected, or swallowed.

components.note: 犭 (dog) — an old link behind 独's meaning 'alone, single, solitary'
虫 (chóng) gives a loose sound connection to 独's reading dú
立 depicts a person standing with arms and legs spread, on a horizontal line representing the ground — a simple picture of standing upright.

example.hanzi: 这个国家最终获得了独立。
example.pinyin: Zhège guójiā zuìzhōng huòdé le dúlì.
example.english: This country finally gained independence.
example.fact: 独立 literally means "to stand alone" — 独 ("single, solitary") plus 立 (a pictograph of a person standing upright on the ground) — and covers the same ground in Chinese that English splits between a nation's political independence and a person's personal self-reliance, both expressed with this one compound.

components.note: 至 (zhì, to arrive) — carries 到's core meaning, 'to reach, to arrive'
刂 (a form of 刀, dāo) gives a sound close to 到's pronunciation dào
Originally depicted a wheat plant; this agricultural picture was borrowed early on to represent the unrelated verb 'to come.'

example.hanzi: 大家都在期待春天的到来。
example.pinyin: Dàjiā dōu zài qídài chūntiān de dàolái.
example.english: Everyone is looking forward to the arrival of spring.
example.fact: 到来 often functions almost like a noun, especially in the pattern ...的到来 ("the advent/arrival of...") used for the onset of a season, era, or event — carrying a touch more weight or ceremony than the plainer verb 到 or 来到, which read as a simpler, everyday "to arrive."

example.hanzi: 这个数据不对,你查查看。
example.pinyin: Zhège shùjù bú duì, nǐ chácha kàn.
example.english: This data is wrong — go check it.
example.fact: 查查 doubles the verb 查 ("to check, look up") the same way 看看 doubles 看 ("to look") — Mandarin's common VV pattern that turns a command into something more casual, "just go take a quick look," rather than a heavier, formal order to investigate; it's often extended to 查查看, tacking on 看 ("and see") for the same casual effect.

components.note: 贝 (shell, an ancient form of money) — 赛 originally related to offering valuables, later coming to mean 'to compete.'
宀 (mián) gives a sound distantly related to sài, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 我们的球队进入了这次比赛的决赛。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen de qiúduì jìnrù le zhècì bǐsài de juésài.
example.english: Our team advanced to the finals of this competition.
example.fact: 决赛 literally means "the decisive match" — 决 ("to decide, settle") plus 赛 ("competition") — sitting at the top of a family of tournament-stage words built the same way: 初赛 ("preliminary round"), 半决赛 ("semifinal," literally "half-decisive-match"), and 决赛 itself, the final round that settles everything.

components.note: 手 is a simple picture of an open hand with the fingers spread out.
段 shows 殳 (a hand wielding a tool) cutting or shaping stone into pieces — giving 段 its meaning 'section, segment, paragraph.'

example.hanzi: 他用了各种手段来达到自己的目的。
example.pinyin: Tā yòng le gèzhǒng shǒuduàn lái dádào zìjǐ de mùdì.
example.english: He used every kind of means to achieve his own goal.
example.fact: 手段 sits on a sliding scale from neutral "method" to outright "scheming" depending on context — 谈判手段 ("negotiating tactics") is fine, but 使手段 ("to pull tricks") is openly critical — a shade of cunning its more purely neutral near-synonym 方法 ("method, approach") doesn't carry.

components.note: 页 (head) — 顾 originally related to turning the head to look back at something
厄 (è) gives a sound distantly related to 顾's reading gù, having drifted apart over time
宀 (roof) — represents a home.
各 (each, various) — a person arriving from elsewhere and welcomed under one's roof gave 客 its meaning 'guest, visitor.'

example.hanzi: 这家商店的顾客非常多。
example.pinyin: Zhèjiā shāngdiàn de gùkè fēicháng duō.
example.english: This store has a huge number of customers.
example.fact: 客 (literally "guest," someone welcomed under a roof) turns up as a suffix across a whole family of words for visitors and users — 顾客 ("customer," someone "looked after" as a guest), 游客 ("tourist"), 房客 ("tenant, lodger") — framing each relationship through the lens of hospitality rather than transaction.

components.note: 农 is the simplified form of 農, which depicted using a hoe 辰 to till a field 田 — an image of farming that gave rise to the meaning 'agriculture.'
土 (earth) — 场 relates to a flat open area of ground, such as a field or venue.
昜 (yáng) gives a hint of the sound — 场 is pronounced chǎng, a connection that has drifted significantly over time.

example.hanzi: 爷爷在乡下有一个小农场。
example.pinyin: Yéye zài xiāngxià yǒu yí gè xiǎo nóngchǎng.
example.english: Grandpa has a small farm out in the countryside.
example.fact: 场 (literally "an open plot of ground") is a productive suffix for naming venues built on open space — 农场 ("farm"), 操场 ("sports field"), 停车场 ("parking lot") — all reusing the same character for a flat, open-air area, just filled with a different purpose each time.

components.note: 网 depicts a woven mesh net stretched over a frame — a picture of a fishing or hunting net, giving 网 its meaning 'net, network.'
纟 (thread) — 络 relates to threads woven together into a net or web.
各 (gè) gives a sound distantly related to luò, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 现在几乎每个人都离不开网络。
example.pinyin: Xiànzài jīhū měi gè rén dōu lí bu kāi wǎngluò.
example.english: Nowadays almost everyone can't do without the Internet.
example.fact: 网 is a pictograph of a woven net, and 络 (built on the thread radical 纟) names an interconnected web of threads or veins — together 网络 already meant "a connected mesh" well before computers existed, which is why the word slotted so naturally onto "network" and "the Internet" once the technology arrived.

components.note: 口 is a simple picture of an open mouth.
衣 (clothing) — 袋 names something made of cloth or similar material, a bag.
代 (dài) is an exact match for the sound of 袋.

example.hanzi: 他把钥匙放进了裤子口袋里。
example.pinyin: Tā bǎ yàoshi fàngjìn le kùzi kǒudài lǐ.
example.english: He put the keys into his pants pocket.
example.fact: 口 ("mouth, opening") plus 袋 ("bag," built on the clothing radical 衣) literally describes a pocket or sack by its most functional feature — the opening you reach into — the same logic behind other 口-compounds like 瓶口 ("the mouth of a bottle") and 门口 ("doorway, entrance").

example.hanzi: 手机让我们的生活变得更加方便。
example.pinyin: Shǒujī ràng wǒmen de shēnghuó biàn de gèngjiā fāngbiàn.
example.english: Smartphones have made our lives more convenient.
example.fact: Beyond meaning "convenient," 方便 doubles as Mandarin's most common polite euphemism for using the restroom — 我想去方便一下 ("I'd like to go and, ah, take care of things") sidesteps blunter terms, the same instinct behind English stand-ins like "powder my nose."

components.note: 日 (sun/day) — relates to 时's meaning of 'time, season'; the phonetic part of the character was later replaced by 寸 in the simplified form
木 (wood) — 机 originally referred to a wooden device or machine, such as a loom.
几 depicts a small table or stool — combined with 木 (wood), the character pictured a wooden machine or mechanism.

example.hanzi: 现在正是投资的好时机。
example.pinyin: Xiànzài zhèng shì tóuzī de hǎo shíjī.
example.english: Right now is a great opportunity for investment.
example.fact: 时机 zeroes in specifically on timing — the moment being right for something, as in 抓住时机 ("seize the opportune moment") — while its broader near-synonym 机会 ("opportunity, chance") just names a favorable chance existing at all, without necessarily emphasizing when.

components.note: 疒 (sickness) — relates directly to 病's meaning 'illness, disease, to be sick.'
丙 (bǐng) gives a sound hint — 病 is pronounced bìng, sharing the same base sound with a different tone.

example.hanzi: 这台电脑最近总出毛病。
example.pinyin: Zhètái diànnǎo zuìjìn zǒng chū máobìng.
example.english: This computer has kept having problems lately.
example.fact: 毛病 stretches informally across three different kinds of trouble that English keeps as separate words — a mechanical glitch (电脑出毛病, "the computer's acting up"), a recurring health ailment (老毛病), and a personal character flaw (坏毛病, "a bad habit") — all covered by this one colloquial term.

components.note: 爪 (a hand/claw) — pressing down.
卩 depicts a seal or stamp — a hand pressing a seal down gave 印 its meaning 'to print, seal, stamp.'
广 (a building or shelter) — 度 pictures people gathering indoors.
廿 (twenty) — a group of people meeting to measure or deliberate gave 度 its meaning of a 'degree' or 'measure,' as in temperature or angles.

example.hanzi: 印度是世界上人口最多的国家之一。
example.pinyin: Yìndù shì shìjiè shàng rénkǒu zuì duō de guójiā zhīyī.
example.english: India is one of the most populous countries in the world.
example.fact: 印度 comes from a phonetic transliteration that the Tang-dynasty monk Xuanzang recorded in his travelogue 大唐西域记 as a more accurate rendering of the local name than earlier Chinese terms like 身毒 — an older name, 天竺, remained in popular use for centuries afterward regardless, most famously in the novel Journey to the West.

components.note: Depicts a person standing with legs crossed — the crossing shape gave 交 its meaning 'to intersect, exchange, hand over.'
氵 (water) — relates directly to 流's meaning 'to flow.'
㐬 (liú) gives the sound — 流 is also pronounced liú, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 两国之间的文化交流越来越多。
example.pinyin: Liǎngguó zhījiān de wénhuà jiāoliú yuè lái yuè duō.
example.english: Cultural exchange between the two countries is increasing.
example.fact: 交 pictures a person standing with legs crossed — an image of intersection and exchange — and 流 means "to flow" (built on the water radical 氵); 交流 combines them into "crossing and flowing," an image of back-and-forth movement equally apt for river currents and for a genuine two-way conversation.

components.note: 讠 (speech, words) — the middle of the character, an exchange of talk.
辛 (bitter, sharp), placed on both sides, representing the two disputing parties, together giving 辩 its meaning 'to argue, debate.'
扌 (hand) — represents the act of guarding or defending.
户 (door/household) — protecting one's home gave 护 its meaning 'to protect, guard.'

example.hanzi: 律师在法庭上为被告辩护。
example.pinyin: Lǜshī zài fǎtíng shàng wèi bèigào biànhù.
example.english: The lawyer argued in defense of the defendant in court.
example.fact: 辩护 specifically names defending someone through argument or speech — a lawyer's courtroom defense, or defending a position in a debate — while 保护 ("to protect") covers physical or practical shielding from harm; English's single word "defend" blurs a distinction Chinese keeps clearly separate.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 打 relates to hitting or performing an action with the hand.
丁 (dīng) gives the sound — 打 is pronounced dǎ, a connection that has shifted in tone.
扌 (hand) — dressing up and costuming traditionally involve the hands.
分 (fēn) gives a sound distantly related to bàn, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 她精心打扮,准备去参加婚礼。
example.pinyin: Tā jīngxīn dǎban, zhǔnbèi qù cānjiā hūnlǐ.
example.english: She dressed up carefully, getting ready to attend the wedding.
example.fact: 打 in 打扮 functions as one of Mandarin's most productive "light verbs" — the same 打 that appears in 打电话 ("make a phone call") and 打篮球 ("play basketball") — contributing almost no meaning of its own beyond loosely signaling "to do, to perform," which trips up learners who expect 打 to always mean "to hit."

components.note: 走 (to walk/run) — 起 relates to standing up and setting into motion.
己 (jǐ) gives a close sound cue — 起 is pronounced qǐ, sharing the same final sound.
石 (stone) — 码 originally related to counting stones used for reckoning, extended to mean 'number, code.'
马 (mǎ) is an exact match for the sound of 码.

example.hanzi: 这件事起码需要三天才能完成。
example.pinyin: Zhèjiàn shì qǐmǎ xūyào sān tiān cái néng wánchéng.
example.english: This task will take at least three days to finish.
example.fact: 码 broadly means "a numerical marker or code" (号码 "number," 密码 "password"), so 起码 literally suggests "the starting mark" — a baseline value things don't fall below — which lines up neatly with its modern sense as an adverb meaning "at the very least."

components.note: Woman — an old semantic root sometimes linked to feelings.
Gives the sound jiān, related to xián but drifted apart over time.
犭 (dog) — 犯 originally related to a dog attacking, later extended to any act of violation
㔾 (jié) gives a sound distantly related to 犯's reading fàn, having drifted apart over time

example.hanzi: 警方正在寻找这起案件的嫌犯。
example.pinyin: Jǐngfāng zhèngzài xúnzhǎo zhèqǐ ànjiàn de xiánfàn.
example.english: The police are currently searching for the suspect in this case.
example.fact: 嫌犯 is a shortened form of the fuller legal term 嫌疑犯 ("suspected criminal") — 嫌 means "to suspect, to doubt" — so it names someone merely under suspicion, legally and linguistically distinct from 犯人 ("convict"), the word reserved for someone already found guilty.

components.note: 八 here depicts something splitting apart or being divided.
厶 is an old form meaning 'private' or 'one's own' — 公 shows dividing up private property to share it fairly, giving rise to the meaning 'public' or 'fair.'
廾 (two hands) — depicts hands at work.
一 represents the latch or bar of a door; hands lifting it away gave 开 its meaning 'to open, to start.'

example.hanzi: 这个消息还没有公开。
example.pinyin: Zhège xiāoxi hái méiyǒu gōngkāi.
example.english: This piece of news hasn't been made public yet.
example.fact: 公开 does triple grammatical duty — adjective ("public," as in 公开的信息 "public information"), verb ("to make public, to reveal," as in 公开这个消息 "release this news"), and adverb ("openly," as in 公开反对 "openly oppose") — one word covering categories English splits into three separate terms.

components.note: 彳 depicts a step with the left foot; together with 亍 (a step with the right foot), 行 shows a person walking or moving.
亍 depicts a step with the right foot, complementing 彳 to form the idea of walking or travel.
木 (tree) — 李 is the plum tree, a type of fruit tree
子 (zǐ) gives a sound close to 李's reading lǐ

example.hanzi: 上飞机前,请检查一下你的行李。
example.pinyin: Shàng fēijī qián, qǐng jiǎnchá yíxià nǐ de xíngli.
example.english: Before boarding the plane, please check your luggage.
example.fact: 行 ("to travel") carries the obvious half of the meaning, but 李 here is generally understood to be a phonetic loan unrelated to its everyday sense "plum" (or the common surname Li) — some accounts trace 行李 back to an older form 行理, "travel affairs," with 李 gradually substituting for 理 as a sound-alike character.

components.note: 王 (jade, written as the radical for 玉) — 玛 names a type of precious stone, agate.
马 (mǎ) is an exact match for the sound of 玛.
丽 is the simplified form of 麗, which depicted the ornate antlers of a deer (鹿) — a fitting image behind its meaning 'beautiful, magnificent.'

example.hanzi: 玛丽是我在美国认识的一个朋友。
example.pinyin: Mǎlì shì wǒ zài Měiguó rènshi de yí gè péngyou.
example.english: Mary is a friend I met in the United States.
example.fact: 玛丽 is a phonetic transliteration chosen for sound but also for flattering meaning — 玛 ("agate," a gemstone written with the jade radical 王) and 丽 ("beautiful," from an older character depicting a deer's ornate antlers) — a common double duty when rendering foreign women's names into Chinese, picking characters that sound right and read as attractive.
